facts.text: Pitkin began life as Quartzville, Colorado’s first mining camp west of the Continental Divide, founded in 1879 by three miners.
The town sits on a one‑mile alpine meadow at 9,242 feet, overlooking Quartz Creek where the North, South, and Middle Fox Creeks converge.
Pitkin’s name honors former Colorado Governor Frederick W. Pitkin, a Connecticut native who moved west for health reasons and helped shape the region.
A 1,772‑foot narrow‑gauge railroad tunnel, the Alpine Tunnel, cuts through the Continental Divide just thirty miles from town, once part of the Denver & South Platte line.
Founded in 1879, Pitkin was incorporated on August 11 of that year, marking its transition from a mining camp to an official statutory town.
